clinicalPearls: A conjugate horizontal jerk nystagmus that appears or intensifies when one eye is occluded, now termed fusion maldevelopment nystagmus syndrome
The fast phase beats toward the viewing (uncovered) eye, reversing direction depending on which eye fixates
It is strongly associated with early disruption of binocular vision, such as infantile esotropia and dissociated vertical deviation
When some nystagmus is present even with both eyes open it is called manifest latent nystagmus
Covering one eye to measure visual acuity can worsen the nystagmus and falsely reduce the measured acuity
Recognition matters mainly to avoid misinterpreting it as a sign of intracranial disease
reference.pathophysiology: Latent nystagmus arises from maldevelopment of binocular fusion during early infancy, typically in the context of infantile strabismus, which disturbs the normal cortical monocular motion processing that underlies gaze holding. Monocular occlusion unbalances this system and elicits a jerk nystagmus whose fast phase beats toward the fixating eye. The condition reflects a developmental abnormality of the visual motion pathways rather than an acquired brainstem or cerebellar lesion.
additionalInvestigations: Orthoptic assessment of ocular alignment and fusion
Careful acuity testing that avoids full occlusion (using a fogging lens)
Documentation of the nystagmus with each eye fixating
Assessment for associated infantile esotropia and dissociated vertical deviation
Eye-movement recording where diagnostic doubt persists
redFlags: Vertical or purely torsional nystagmus suggesting central disease
New onset in an older child or adult
Optic atrophy or other afferent pathway signs
reference.prognosis: The condition itself is benign and stable; visual outcome depends on the associated strabismus and amblyopia, which should be managed on their own merits.
pitfalls: Underestimating acuity by fully occluding one eye during testing
Mistaking it for acquired nystagmus and ordering unnecessary imaging
Missing the associated infantile strabismus and amblyopia
Confusing manifest latent nystagmus with congenital nystagmus syndrome
references: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: There is no drug therapy; management targets the underlying infantile strabismus and any amblyopia on their own merits
Treat amblyopia with occlusion or atropine penalisation, but avoid abrupt full occlusion which intensifies the nystagmus, favouring fogging or partial penalisation
Correct significant refractive error with spectacles to optimise vision
Offer strabismus surgery for the associated infantile esotropia or dissociated vertical deviation as indicated
Test acuity monocularly using a fogging lens rather than a full occluder to avoid falsely reducing measured vision
Recognise the benign developmental nature to avoid unnecessary neuroimaging, and follow up with orthoptic assessment
